items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1975-02-03
items.q: we made the Kingsville Parade with Johnny Wiggs and Raymond Burke... I believe, didn't you go out with us to Biloxi one night with Wiggs and Raymond Burke? ... session that was called Doc and His Patience with the two clarinets, Raymond Burke

ctx.x: Well, he must have heard several tones. There's another Harry Smith that I've heard of somewhere. Well, did you ever do any recording sessions in New Orleans?

Oh, yeah, of course. Well of course I did a lot of recording sessions in cooperation with Joe Merez. Some of them were mine, some of them were his. And I think I recall that you were present at some of the sessions. I think you were at Woodman of the World Hall when we made the Kingsville Parade with Johnny Wiggs and Raymond Burke and Emil Christian, Jeff Riddick, Paul Barberan, Sherwood Mangiapani.

I came to the Woodman of the World for the dances, and I think I was there for the recording session. I think you were. Those two things get mixed up in my mind. We were talking about that once and how you didn't have the same personnel.

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1975-02-03
items.q: Of course I've recorded Rayman a lot.

ctx.x: Yeah, I find that, in a way, how many, I find this hard to sort out in my mind, because I'm trying to sort out all the different Wiggs's in my mind, and your opinion of the different Wiggs's, our opinions.

Well, of course I always like Wiggs better when he gets the Davenport out of the horn. And I have found that in the right kind of a musical environment he does that. It always seems to me that he plays like Oliver when he's happy and like Bix when he's mad. And I find even that interesting, and I found Bix interesting enough. But, I'm not excited by that, you know, I'm not excited by that. I'm more excited by that, you know, I'm more interested than excited by that. But of course Wiggs, you see, having gone…
a jazz organization. You could listen to him as a solo I see.

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1976-02-19
items.q: if you didn't already know the existing body of work and you were to hear uh solos by Edmund Hall and Raymond Burke it would be uh virtually impossible for you to determine which one was the white one which one was the black one

ctx.x: but when some of those solos uh come through the early

the early things didn't even have the solos yeah there was no way that you could tell so so that uh no longer becomes a consideration and of course there were many white musicians and and still are white musicians who are not distinguishable in their sounds from black ones for example if you didn't already know the existing body of work and you were to hear uh solos by Edmund Hall and Raymond Burke it would be uh virtually impossible for you to determine which one was the white one which one was the black one…
mm-hmm but wouldn't it be fair to say that there are certain styles like the Chicago style that was predominantly a white style
